| Defense-related portion of the reviewed appellate judgment | Vacated and remanded, 7–2 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Scalia and Thomas would remove the statutory remedial basis on their contrary liability ground | Reconsider the defense and consequent prospective relief under the controlling resource rule; Stevens agrees in this judgment only, and Kennedy relies on his separate ground |

The district court, through the appellate remand, must determine appropriate services and the fundamental-alteration defense in light of available resources and the needs of others. Relief must be effective for these respondents and confined to the supported lawful record. The continuing injunction is subject to lawful lower-court administration; vacatur does not automatically terminate community services or direct readmission. The later January 1999 district judgment is not independently reviewed or vacated. Unadjudicated constitutional claims remain unresolved.

### The enacted fault rule and the meaning of the offense are distinct

#### Peoples Rights Organization, Inc. v. City of Columbus

**Docket or dockets:** Sixth Circuit Nos. 96-3468 and 96-3495; 152 F.3d 522. No separately established Supreme Court docket.
**Decided:** 1998-10-15.

##### The enacted fault rule and the meaning of the offense are distinct

**Holding:** Section 2323.31(A)'s silence does not plainly negate section 2301.21(B)'s enacted recklessness default: culpability is unnecessary only where the offense plainly indicates strict liability; otherwise recklessness suffices for the silent offense. In applying these definitions, the City must prove heedless indifference and perverse disregard of a known risk that the prohibited circumstance was likely to exist; that fault condition can address ignorance of an intelligibly defined characteristic but cannot supply an undefined legal boundary.

**Proposition-level authority:** Thomas's opinion of the Court; O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer join in full, and Stevens joins every part except Part IX. Eight direct joins support this proposition unless Part IX is specified.

##### An existing compatible rifle magazine supplies an intelligible criterion

**Holding:** Section 2323.11(G)(1) identifies a semiautomatic center-fire rifle or carbine accepting an existing detachable magazine with capacity of twenty rounds or more, whether or not its owner possesses that magazine. A merely imaginable future magazine does not establish that physical characteristic, and the City must separately establish the enacted fault condition; the presented categorical vagueness challenge fails on that construction.

**Proposition-level authority:** Thomas's opinion of the Court; O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer join in full, and Stevens joins every part except Part IX. Eight direct joins support this proposition unless Part IX is specified.

##### Shotgun capacity concerns actual compatible ammunition

**Holding:** Section 2323.11(G)(2) covers a semiautomatic shotgun whose magazine accepts more than six rounds of actual compatible ammunition, subject to the enacted fault condition. Different lengths of compatible shells do not make that physical-capacity criterion facially unintelligible; imaginary ammunition or an unproved alteration cannot establish it.

**Proposition-level authority:** Thomas's opinion of the Court; O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer join in full, and Stevens joins every part except Part IX. Eight direct joins support this proposition unless Part IX is specified.

##### Both modification branches lack the relationship that defines the offense

**Holding:** Section 2323.11(G)(3)(a)'s two branches—semiautomatic handguns that are modifications of the referenced rifle or of an automatic firearm—are invalid as written because they fail to identify whether actual conversion, design descent or resemblance makes the handgun prohibited. Recklessness does not cure that missing legal relationship, and dependent restoration or parts references cannot independently impose liability through those invalid branches.

**Proposition-level authority:** Thomas's opinion of the Court; O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer join in full, and Stevens joins every part except Part IX. Eight direct joins support this proposition unless Part IX is specified.

##### Original handgun design is distinct from undefined modification

**Holding:** Section 2323.11(G)(3)(b) asks whether a semiautomatic handgun was originally designed to accept a detachable magazine holding more than twenty rounds, subject to separate fault. That objective historical criterion is not facially invalid merely because design-history proof may be difficult, and it does not extend to every subsequently conceivable magazine.

**Proposition-level authority:** Thomas's opinion of the Court; O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer join in full, and Stevens joins every part except Part IX. Eight direct joins support this proposition unless Part IX is specified.

##### Restoration requires a former condition and actual capacity of return

**Holding:** Section 2323.11(G)(4) reaches an existing firearm capable of restoration to a former operable condition satisfying an independently valid (G)(1), (G)(2) or (G)(3)(b) definition, with separate fault. It does not permit enforcement based on an invalid modification predicate, raw materials treated as a restored firearm, or unsupported theoretical reconstruction.

**Proposition-level authority:** Thomas's opinion of the Court; O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer join in full, and Stevens joins every part except Part IX. Eight direct joins support this proposition unless Part IX is specified.

##### The two parts branches retain different conditions

**Holding:** The first branch of section 2323.11(G)(5) requires a part or combination designed or intended to convert a firearm into a weapon satisfying a valid (G)(1), (G)(2) or (G)(3)(b) predicate; objective conversion design or the identified conversion purpose must connect the parts to that result. The second requires a combination from which such a weapon may readily be assembled, possessed or controlled by the same person; practical assembly and separate fault remain necessary, and invalid modification predicates cannot independently support either branch.

**Proposition-level authority:** Thomas's opinion of the Court; O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer join in full, and Stevens joins every part except Part IX. Eight direct joins support this proposition unless Part IX is specified.

##### The former-city-registration selectors survive the presented equality challenge

**Holding:** Section 2323.31(B)(3) may exempt a person who lawfully possessed and actually registered that particular assault weapon under former section 2323.05 in 1989, and section 2323.32(B)(2) may exempt a magazine belonging to or forming part of an assault weapon registered under former section 2323.05(C). Protecting that documented registration reliance while limiting the exempt stock rationally supports those selectors under the presented ordinary equality challenge, despite the former ordinance's invalidity and the expired window.

**Proposition-level authority:** Thomas's opinion of the Court, Part IX, joined by O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer (seven Justices). Stevens and Stone-Zsela do not join this proposition.

##### The other magazine exceptions retain their full alternatives

**Holding:** Against the presented ordinary equality challenge, section 2323.32(B)(2) may exempt a large-capacity magazine belonging to an NFA-registered firearm or possessed by the owner of such a firearm; the owner alternative requires neither that the magazine itself be registered nor that it fit that firearm. The separate inert-object branch covers a magazine belonging to or forming part of an assault weapon rendered totally inoperable or inert, which cannot readily be rendered operable or activated and is kept as a trophy, souvenir, curio or museum piece; ownership of an unrelated inert object is insufficient.

**Proposition-level authority:** Thomas's opinion of the Court; O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer join in full, and Stevens joins every part except Part IX. Eight direct joins support this proposition unless Part IX is specified.

##### Relief follows the invalid branches and actual Ohio severability

**Holding:** The invalidity of the two modification branches does not itself eliminate every other definition or exception. The lower courts must determine Ohio severability of those branches and their dependent references, then conform declaratory and injunctive relief to that determination and the component judgments; no enforcement may rest independently on an invalid modification predicate.

**Proposition-level authority:** Thomas's opinion of the Court; O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer join in full, and Stevens joins every part except Part IX. Eight direct joins support this proposition unless Part IX is specified.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No substantive Second Amendment judgment, prosecution, automatic arrest authorization or new registration opportunity follows. No enforcement may rest independently on either invalid modification branch; valid definitions remain subject to the distinct enacted fault condition. Actual Ohio severability determines the conforming declaratory and injunctive relief.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- **Lujan:** applied for concrete injury, causation, redressability and the actual record; unsupported future plans remain insufficient.
- **Abbott Laboratories** and **Babbitt:** applied to present restraints and credible enforcement threats, without requiring prosecution first.
- **Hunt** and **United Food:** applied for representative prospective relief at the actual member-injury scope; United Food's statutory participation exception is not generalized.
- **Grayned:** applied to fair notice and practical enforcement standards; a factual dispute or borderline application is not automatically an absent legal criterion.
- **Kolender:** applied to the independent lack of enforcement guidance in the two modification branches, supporting their invalidity as written.
- **Hoffman Estates:** applied with its context, fault and protected-activity qualifications; its commercial formulation does not erase those premises.
- **Fargo** and **Women's Medical:** applied for separate definition, fault and substantive-validity inquiries; their abortion-specific facial-review rules are not transplanted. Women's Medical also supplies actual Ohio severability analysis.
- **Staples:** applied for characteristic-specific culpability analysis, without importing its federal statutory knowledge requirement or a knowledge-of-illegality rule.
- **Posters 'N' Things:** applied to objective design and distinct relevant knowledge; its complete federal knowledge rule and disputed exclusive intended-use construction are not imposed on the ordinance.
- **Love, Hale, Rybar and Wright:** preserve personal arms invocation and the distinction between a right and a particular restriction; their remands supply no automatic remand or substantive result here.
- **Nordlinger:** its independent reliance holding supports protection of documented expectations, without contractual immunity or a requirement that every grandfather classification survive.
- **Dukes:** applied for a bounded grandfather protection of established reliance.
- **Beach:** applied for rational legislative latitude without converting the test into permission for an unrelated distinction.
- **Heller** and **Romer:** applied to require a relation between the actual classification and its stated purpose, without exact tailoring or a new comprehensive scrutiny tier.
- **Fraternal Order of Police** and **Hiley:** their specific official-use and conviction-relief classifications remain in force; neither resolves the different municipal registry on its own.
- **Springfield Armory**, the earlier Sixth Circuit decision: its invalidation of the former ordinance remains the historical legal setting; its suggested possibility of clearer generic definitions is not advance approval of this ordinance. **Arnold v. City of Cleveland** resolved a distinct Ohio constitutional challenge and supplies no controlling vagueness construction here.

No Supreme Court precedent is overruled. The lower court's collective-only, no-incorporation premise is displaced by Love; its broad strict-liability and categorical-definition reasoning is rejected at the stated scopes.

For the other questions in Peoples Rights Organization, Inc. v. City of Columbus, decided 1998-10-15, Sixth Circuit Nos. 96-3468 and 96-3495; 152 F.3d 522. No separately established Supreme Court docket., see Federal Courts.

### 1. Stabilization has no additional improper-motive element

#### Roberts v. Galen of Virginia, Inc.

**Docket or dockets:** No. 97-53.
**Decided:** 1999-01-13.

##### 1. Stabilization has no additional improper-motive element

**Holding:** A claim under 42 U.S.C. §1395dd(b) does not require proof that a participating hospital acted with an improper financial or other invidious motive. Liability nevertheless requires proof of the enacted stabilization or transfer duty and the applicable civil-action predicates; removing the extra motive requirement establishes neither breach nor injury.

**Proposition-level authority:** The per curiam opinion is joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. All nine adopt both holdings and their stated limits.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Subsection (b)(2) deems the treatment requirement satisfied when the hospital offers the required examination and treatment, informs the patient or representative of their risks and benefits, and that person refuses; the hospital must take all reasonable steps to obtain written informed refusal. Subsection (b)(3) separately addresses refusal of a transfer offered in accordance with subsection (c), after risk-and-benefit information, with the same reasonable-efforts duty concerning written informed refusal. Neither provision is a finding about this patient.

For an unstabilized emergency condition, subsection (c)(1) separately requires either a written transfer request made by the individual or legally responsible representative after receiving information about the hospital's EMTALA duties and the risks of transfer, or a physician's signed certification, based on the information available when transfer occurs, that the expected medical benefits of appropriate treatment elsewhere outweigh the increased transfer risks, including risks to the unborn child in labor; it also requires an appropriate transfer. If no physician is physically present in the emergency department, a medical person qualified under the Secretary's regulations may sign after consultation with a physician who makes the required determination and later countersigns. The certification must summarize its supporting risks and benefits. Appropriate transfer requires risk-minimizing treatment within the transferring hospital's capacity; available receiving space, qualified personnel and acceptance with appropriate treatment; transmission of all emergency-condition records available at transfer, including the condition, observed signs or symptoms, preliminary diagnosis, treatment, test results and written request or certification, together with the name and address of an on-call physician who refused or did not appear within a reasonable time to provide necessary stabilization; qualified personnel and transportation equipment, including necessary and medically appropriate life support during transfer; and any further applicable regulatory conditions. None is declared satisfied or violated here.

Subsection (d)(2)(A) permits the person directly harmed by a participating hospital's violation to sue that hospital for personal-injury damages available under the law of its State and appropriate equitable relief. The separate limitation is two years after the violation. This decision creates no personal action against an individual physician and no automatic liability for later deterioration.

##### 2. The motive-based summary judgment must be reversed; other predicates remain open

**Holding:** Summary judgment rejecting the stabilization claim because the guardian failed to establish improper motive rests on an element the statute does not contain and must be reversed. The hospital's actual-knowledge and completed-screening defenses remain open for lawful consideration on remand; neither is accepted or rejected on its merits by this decision.

**Proposition-level authority:** The same unanimous per curiam opinion controls this confined reversal and remand.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Whether an emergency medical condition existed, what the hospital determined or knew, duration of any duty, stabilization, authorized transfer, causal injury, damages and ultimate liability remain undecided. The treatment-refusal, transfer-refusal and transfer-certification provisions remain distinct; no exception is presumed.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- **National Organization for Women, Inc. v. Scheidler (January 24, 1994):** Applied by analogy for refusal to add an omitted motive element while preserving every enacted liability condition. Its RICO construction remains distinct from EMTALA.
- **Cleland v. Bronson Health Care Group, 917 F.2d 266 (6th Cir. 1990):** The extension of its screening-motivation analysis to impose an extra element under subsection (b) is rejected. The Court does not decide subsection (a)'s screening-motive question.
- **United States v. X-Citement Video, Inc. (November 29, 1994):** Its favorable-judgment defense rule is respected without treating an unestablished alternative factual premise as proved. Neither alternative defense is conclusively adjudicated here.

**Limits and questions not reached:** EMTALA stabilization litigation proceeds without an additional improper-purpose element. The statutory determination, treatment or lawful-transfer conditions, direct personal harm, causation, permitted remedies and limitations period retain their independent force. Screening, stabilization and the separate state-law agency claim remain distinct. The judgment changes no general medical-negligence rule and awards no relief beyond reversal and remand of the appealed stabilization disposition.

**Operative remedy or transition:** **Reversed and remanded, 9–0.** Supporting: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. The reversal removes the improper-motive ground for summary judgment. The actual-knowledge and completed-screening defenses remain open, as do the statute's other predicates and available remedies. The separate state ostensible-agency ruling and other claims are not reopened; no liability judgment, damages award or mandatory trial is ordered.

### Bona fide new citizens receive equal ordinary welfare treatment

#### Saenz v. Roe

**Docket or dockets:** No. 98-97; judgment below, Roe v. Anderson, 134 F.3d 1400.
**Decided:** 1999-05-17.

##### Bona fide new citizens receive equal ordinary welfare treatment

**Holding:** A United States citizen who establishes bona fide residence in a State becomes its citizen on equal terms; the Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship and Privileges or Immunities provisions forbid lowering that otherwise eligible citizen's ordinary welfare benefits solely because of recent arrival or the former State's benefit amount. California's first-year differential violates that guarantee even if the person never received benefits before moving or moved for reasons unrelated to assistance.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer (eight Justices).

##### Federal permission cannot lower the constitutional floor

**Holding:** Congress may structure and condition federal welfare assistance, but may not authorize a State to violate the Fourteenth Amendment's equal-citizenship guarantee. Section 604(c)'s permission to use prior-State benefit levels therefore cannot sustain California's unconstitutional differential; permission is not a federal command.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer (eight Justices).

**Limits and questions not reached:** Bona fide residence verification and equal eligibility conditions remain enforceable. The Court establishes no national benefit amount or general welfare entitlement and does not reopen Slaughter-House's broader construction.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Affirm the preliminary injunction against California's first-year prior-State ceiling; no permanent decree, damages or fixed benefit amount is entered.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- The Slaughter-House Cases supply the specific recognition of becoming another State's citizen through bona fide residence; their broader construction is not reopened.
- Shapiro v. Thompson supplies the prohibition on durational welfare penalties; a reduced payment still burdens current equality.
- Dunn v. Blumstein distinguishes actual residence from additional duration.
- Zobel v. Williams rejects ordinary resident-benefit allocation by arrival history.
- City of Boerne v. Flores prevents statutory replacement of constitutional content.
- Lunding and Romer retain their source-specific equality rules; neither is converted into a general judicial guarantee of welfare amounts.

### The presented facial vagueness challenge fails

#### Schleifer v. City of Charlottesville

**Docket or dockets:** No. 98-1146; review of 159 F.3d 843 (4th Cir. 1998).
**Decided:** 1999-06-15.

##### The presented facial vagueness challenge fails

**Holding:** A juvenile curfew that specifies age, hours, covered places and the prohibited act of remaining is not facially vague on this record merely because its exception for constitutionally protected First Amendment activity requires legal application in particular encounters. The exception preserves the full constitutional protection; uncertain hypotheticals do not establish that this ordinance's common criminal predicate lacks an intelligible standard, and genuinely distinct unconstitutional applications remain open.

**Proposition-level authority:** O'Connor's Part I, joined by Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer, has eight direct votes for the rule, explanation and limits.

##### The substantive judgment rests on separate grounds

**Authority of the judgment:** Five Justices sustain the judgment rejecting the presented substantive liberty and parental-authority claims. No five join a common full scrutiny rationale: three assume significant interests and find the actual protective fit sufficient, while two apply ordinary review because the asserted entitlement has not been established.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The judgment has O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Breyer; no controlling rationale exists under Marks. O'Connor's Part II has only the three votes of O'Connor, Kennedy and Breyer; Scalia's concurrence has Scalia and Thomas. Neither becomes a Court-wide scrutiny rule through aggregation. The assumed-interest approach does not decide the nonfundamentality proposition, and a restraint failing its fit inquiry could still survive ordinary review. Neither rationale is shown to be the governing logical subset of the other under Marks. The Court therefore enters no general standard for every juvenile curfew or fit-parent objection.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- City of Chicago v. Morales: preserves the requirement of meaningful guidance for the common enforcement predicate and the insufficiency of warnings to cure its absence; distinguishes this ordinance's enacted age, time, place and conduct criteria.
- Peoples Rights Organization v. City of Columbus: applies its distinction between an absent legal criterion and difficulty applying an existing criterion.
- Grayned v. City of Rockford: applies its contextual fair-notice and enforcement-guidance principles.
- Kolender v. Lawson: preserves independent legal constraints on enforcement discretion; assurances of restraint do not replace them.
- Village of Hoffman Estates v. Flipside: applies contextual facial-review and intelligible-core principles without immunizing a genuinely standardless predicate.
- Papachristou v. City of Jacksonville: preserves protection against discretionary criminalization of ordinary public activity; it does not dispense with analysis of this law's defined operation.
- Reno v. ACLU: preserves actual constitutional expression and the boundary against judicial rewriting; its adult-network-speech ruling supplies no automatic scrutiny tier for every juvenile presence law.
- Washington v. Glucksberg: remains claim-specific and supplies no exclusive history-only method governing all liberties; the separate substantive writings here adopt no common extension of its rule.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The ordinance survives the presented challenges and the denial of relief remains effective. Its constitutional-expression exception retains its full reach, and materially different applications remain open. The controlling facial rule distinguishes a missing enforcement criterion from difficult application of a defined law. The divided substantive grounds establish no universal curfew scrutiny formula, unrestricted nighttime entitlement, parental veto or rule validating every prosecution. The family-contact and custody-transition decisions retain their separate settings; no curfew hearing or proof burden is derived from them.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Overall affirmance is 5–4. Supporting: O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Breyer. Opposing: Stone-Zsela would reverse on facial vagueness; Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg would reverse in part on substantive liberty and parental authority.

The facial vagueness/expression theory is rejected 8–1 by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer, with Stone-Zsela dissenting. On the substantive claims, O'Connor, Kennedy and Breyer sustain the judgment on assumed significant interests and case-specific protective fit; Scalia and Thomas sustain it under ordinary review. Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg would grant fitted relief for supported parent-authorized lawful activity. Stone-Zsela does not reach those substantive questions. The affirmed final judgment requires no new injunction, damages award or remedial remand.

### Holding 1— Beneficial mitigation does not eliminate underlying-impairment coverage

#### Sutton v. United Air Lines, Inc.

**Docket or dockets:** No. 97-1943
**Decided:** 1999-06-22.

##### Holding 1— Beneficial mitigation does not eliminate underlying-impairment coverage

**Holding:** Under the original 42 U.S.C. §12102(2)(A), successful mitigating measures do not erase the underlying impairment: whether it substantially limits a major life activity is assessed without treating beneficial correction or medication as eliminating that limitation. The protections of the Americans with Disabilities Act do not disappear because an individual has successfully treated or mitigated an impairment. The existence of a qualifying disability must be distinguished from the individual’s capacity to perform particular employment duties. Effective treatment does not itself establish that the underlying impairment is outside the statute’s protection. Individual proof of substantial limitation remains necessary; this is not a categorical rule that every eyeglass wearer is disabled.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part I of Chief Justice Stone-Zsela’s Opinion of the Court, joined by Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. All five adopt the rule, individualized-proof requirement and separation of coverage from qualification, accommodation and safety.

##### Holding 2 — The actual-disability claim requires reassessment under the underlying-impairment rule

**Holding:** The dismissal of the actual-disability claim is vacated and the claim remanded for reassessment without beneficial mitigation eliminating the underlying visual limitation, with individual proof that the impairment substantially limits seeing. Qualification, reasonable accommodation and legitimate safety defenses must be resolved on their own elements; the remand awards no automatic hiring, reinstatement or accommodation.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part II of the Court’s opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. These five adopt the vacatur and bounded reassessment; O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas dissent from this component.

##### Holding 3 — The alleged perceived restriction is confined to a specialized job category

**Holding:** Assuming working is a major life activity, a regarded-as-working claim requires an alleged perceived restriction in a class or broad range of jobs; exclusion from the specialized global-airline-pilot category alleged here does not suffice. The pleaded exclusion remains insufficient even under the assumption that United rejected these applicants for all of its pilot positions.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part III of the Court’s opinion commands all nine Justices: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. Each joins both the perceived-class rule and the dismissal application.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- **School Board of Nassau County v. Arline:** Applies its functional protection and individualized assessment while keeping disability distinct from qualification and supported exclusion; its actual setting and limits remain intact.
- **Bragdon v. Abbott:** Applies its individualized disability framework and resolves the reserved mitigation question through the underlying-impairment rule. Its reproduction holding, substantial residual-risk application and distinct Title III objective direct-threat rules remain intact.
- **United States v. Haggar Apparel Co. and Chevron:** Preserve actual delegation and statutory fit as conditions of agency deference. The Court rests on its construction of the original ADA and makes no general decision about ADA definitional authority or the binding force of every EEOC regulation or Appendix statement.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Under the original ADA, beneficial mitigating measures do not eliminate an underlying impairment’s substantial limitation for actual-disability coverage. Individual substantiality remains required, and coverage is distinct from qualification, reasonable accommodation and legitimate safety standards. This resolves Bragdon’s express mitigation reservation without automatic coverage for every corrected condition. The actual-seeing claim returns for reassessment under that rule.

Assuming working is a major life activity, the regarded-as theory presented here also fails because the alleged perception concerns a specialized global-airline-pilot category rather than a class or broad range of jobs. Separate coverage branches, individual proof, qualification and lawful defenses retain their distinct elements. No precedent is overruled; no general delegation or airline-safety rule is decided.

**Operative remedy or transition:**

| Judgment component | Disposition and vote | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices |
|---|---|---|---|
| Actual disability — seeing (Parts I–II) | Vacated and remanded, 5–4 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas |
| Regarded as substantially limited in working (Part III) | Affirmed, 9–0 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | — |

The judgment is affirmed in part and vacated in part. The actual-disability claim returns for reassessment without treating beneficial correction as eliminating the underlying limitation; the applicants must establish individual substantial limitation. Qualification, accommodation and legitimate safety defenses are resolved on their own elements. The regarded-as-working dismissal stands. No automatic hiring, reinstatement, accommodation, damages or new evidentiary proceeding is ordered, and no airline hiring criterion is categorically validated.

### Personal invocation does not depend on state-militia affiliation

#### United States v. Wright

**Docket or dockets:** Eleventh Circuit No. 95-8397; judgment below, 117 F.3d 1265. No separately established Supreme Court docket.
**Decided:** 1998-10-05.

##### Personal invocation does not depend on state-militia affiliation

**Holding:** Wright may invoke the personal arms guarantee without proving membership in, service to, or preparation for a militia actively maintained and trained by a State. Military usefulness neither excludes an arm from the guarantee nor gives an unrestricted exemption from regulation; the actual weapon, conduct and restriction must be considered.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stone-Zsela's opinion of the Court; all nine Justices join this holding.

##### Core-Preservation Review governs restrictions on the personal arms right

**Holding:** Stage 1 asks whether the law interferes with protected keeping, bearing, acquisition, necessary ammunition or transportation of arms, with constitutional coverage determined from text, history and the Court's precedents. If protected activity is burdened, Stage 2 requires justification corresponding to the severity of the restriction's practical operation, subject to the independent categorical rule that government may not abolish meaningful possession of ordinary functional defensive arms in the home.

**Operative qualifications:** A core deprivation receives strict scrutiny: the government must establish a compelling interest, narrow tailoring and the absence of a comparably effective, materially less restrictive alternative. A substantial regulation receives intermediate scrutiny: an important governmental objective, a substantial relationship between the regulation and that objective, and a restriction that does not unnecessarily or effectively eliminate the protected activity. An incidental regulation imposing no meaningful interference receives deferential reasonableness review; arbitrary administration, discrimination and cumulative destruction of the right remain unconstitutional. Routine equipment specifications, administrative procedures and minor requirements qualify for that last category only when they do not materially obstruct the right. Actual operation controls: calling an effective prohibition a safety measure or administrative rule cannot reduce its level of review.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part II-B is joined by O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg as well as its author, Stone-Zsela. These five adopt the entire framework, including each tier, the practical-operation rule and the categorical home boundary. The rule is direct majority law, not a synthesis of separate opinions.

**Material application:** Love identifies the personal holder, incorporates the guarantee and protects acquisition necessary to exercise it. Hale requires attention to the actual weapon and keeps coverage distinct from lawful regulation; military usefulness decides neither immunity nor exclusion. Rybar requires a genuine application instead of disposing of the claim through militia affiliation. Those decisions leave the measure of justification open. The Court now supplies that measure because a remand must identify how protected activity and permissible regulation relate. Text and history inform coverage and regulatory limits without creating a closed catalogue. A real individual guarantee requires protection against practical destruction, while regulation that leaves its exercise meaningfully available calls for a justification fitted to its actual burden. Public safety is important, but its invocation alone does not establish that fit. Conversely, recognizing a personal right does not subject every equipment rule or administrative step to strict scrutiny. Registration and a possession prohibition must be examined separately. The home boundary protects a meaningful core; it does not grant immunity to every weapon, person or use. Necessary ammunition and transportation receive protection as incidents of protected keeping or bearing, not through coverage of every item or transport method. That boundary, the graduated standard and the application to particular facts perform different functions.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Prohibiting ordinary functional handguns in the home and effectively eliminating all lawful public carry illustrate core burdens; no particular public-carry law is before the Court. Public-carry licensing, safety instruction, examinations, demonstrated proficiency, refresher training and recertification, including their classification and justification, are expressly reserved. No universal numerical rule, militia exclusion, military-weapon immunity or comprehensive prohibited-arms list is adopted.

##### The machinegun-count affirmance requires both stages in the first instance

**Holding:** When the appellate affirmance of this machinegun conviction materially rests on the invalid affiliation requirement and supplies no adequate independent application of the personal arms guarantee to the actual weapons and restriction, that affirmance must be vacated for the preserved constitutional application. On remand, the lower courts must apply both stages of Core-Preservation Review in the first instance: determine constitutional coverage of the completed automatic weapon under Hale, address the disassembled weapon and its actual statutory branch where material, and then classify and justify any burden on protected activity by its practical operation.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stone-Zsela's Part II-C, joined by O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg, controls the direction to apply both stages of Core-Preservation Review. Stevens, Scalia, Thomas and Breyer also join the vacatur and bounded remand apart from that framework direction; the judgment is unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Only the appellate affirmance of the one section 922(o) count is vacated. The existing record may suffice; ordinary additional proceedings are permitted only as needed. The Court creates no new statutory element, second machinegun count or severance of the conditional plea, and does not reopen admitted possession. It orders no empirical study, hearing, new trial, acquittal, release or return of arms. The alternative jury-instruction request returns only insofar as it remains procedurally material under the preserved plea after lawful disposition of the arms claim; no particular instruction or trial is ordered. This is not an automatic-remand rule for every arms case.

##### The Ninth Amendment supplies no established independent exemption here

**Holding:** Invoking privacy and natural self-defense under the Ninth Amendment does not itself establish an independent constitutional immunity for this machinegun possession and destructive-device nonregistration. The asserted exemption fails without resolving the separately preserved Second Amendment application.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stone-Zsela's opinion of the Court; all nine Justices join this holding.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Core-Preservation Review governs restrictions on protected activity. The tier and ultimate validity of this machinegun restriction remain undecided; no closed weapons catalogue or categorical exclusion of dangerous arms is adopted. The applicable statutory exceptions and registration limits remain intact. The Court orders no acquittal, release, return of arms, new trial, automatic hearing, acceptance adjustment or particular sentence; the machinegun count and sentence return on their distinct grounds. A reserved legal challenge does not immunize false factual denials or other conduct inconsistent with actual acceptance.

For the other questions in United States v. Wright, decided 1998-10-05, Eleventh Circuit No. 95-8397; judgment below, 117 F.3d 1265. No separately established Supreme Court docket., see Constitutional Structure, Criminal Procedure.

### The particular April 1992 application was not sufficiently clear for personal damages

#### Wilson v. Layne

**Docket or dockets:** No. 98-83.
**Decided:** 1999-05-24.

##### The particular April 1992 application was not sufficiently clear for personal damages

**Holding:** The respondent officers receive qualified immunity because, on the April 16, 1992 legal landscape, the particular restriction on accompanying, nonassisting media observers during otherwise authorized warrant execution was not sufficiently clear to impose personal damages liability. The absence of a factually identical case is neither required nor sufficient for immunity; the Court considers the particular application and all relevant conduct-date law while accepting the supported nonassistance facts.

**Proposition-level authority:** Scalia's Part II, joined by O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer (seven Justices).

For the other questions and complete operative scope in Wilson v. Layne, 1999-05-24, No. 98-83, see Criminal Procedure.

### Admissions-process injury and remedies

#### Texas v. Lesage, 528 U.S. 18 (1999)

**Docket or dockets:** No. 98-1111.
**Decided:** November 29, 1999.

##### What a successful same-decision defense defeats after an unconstitutional admissions process

**Holding:** Once an unconstitutional admissions process has been established, the school must prove by a preponderance that a specified constitutional process would have produced the same rejection. Success defeats admission and compensation for that denial and its consequences; it does not erase the separately established unequal-process injury.

**Proposition-level authority:** Unanimous per curiam opinion.

**Material application:** The counterfactual must specify a constitutional admissions process, including race uses controlling law permits. Academic comparisons remain evidence rather than conclusive proof; summary-judgment genuine-dispute requirements apply.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Considering race does not alone establish that the admissions program was unconstitutional. The existing substantial-justification standard and permissible-use boundaries are unchanged.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Hopwood v. Texas supplies the school-borne preponderance burden, specified lawful counterfactual and separation of competitive injury from lost admission. Mt. Healthy supplies the causal distinction through Hopwood.


##### When independent process injury and prospective exposure may support relief

**Holding:** An established unconstitutional process may support nominal or declaratory recognition even if Texas proves the same lawful rejection, but only under an available cause against a proper defendant and subject to immunity. Prospective relief additionally requires concrete continuing or imminent exposure to unequal competition and an equitable basis.

**Proposition-level authority:** Unanimous per curiam opinion.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Reverse only the legal irrelevance ruling and remand for claim-specific adjudication; do not reinstate the entire defense judgment. Sections 1981 and 1983 and Title VI, proper defendants, immunity and remedies require separate treatment. Prospective relief fails absent concrete continuing or imminent exposure; cessation and abandonment must be determined rather than assumed.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Carey v. Piphus distinguishes nominal recognition from compensation for proved loss. Northeastern Florida Chapter v. Jacksonville recognizes unequal competition without guaranteeing selection.

### Intentional individualized unequal treatment

#### Village of Willowbrook v. Olech, 528 U.S. 562

**Docket or dockets:** No. 98-1288.

**Decided:** February 23, 2000.

##### Intentional irrational treatment of an individual may violate equal protection

**Holding:** An individual states an equal-protection claim by alleging intentional differential treatment from materially similarly situated persons without a rational basis for the distinction; membership in a separately identified group is unnecessary. Subjective ill will may be evidence of arbitrariness or pretext, but is not an independent element of this objectively irrational intentional-treatment claim.

**Proposition-level authority:** Justice Stevens's opinion of the Court is joined in full by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; eight directly adopt this rule and the pleading application. Breyer concurs in the judgment on the additional allegation of vindictive action and does not join the objective rule's independent sufficiency.

**Material application:** The complaint's intentional demand for a 33-foot easement, compared with 15 feet for materially similar owners, together with alleged irrationality and arbitrariness, states the claim independently of spite. Alternative reckless-disregard allegations do not replace intent; later acceptance of 15 feet proves neither original irrationality nor liability.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Negligence, ordinary error, discretionary disagreement, material differences and objectively rational distinctions do not suffice. The challenger must negate reasonably conceivable legitimate grounds; no contemporaneous official rationale, heightened scrutiny, reversed burden or evidence-pleading requirement is imposed. The alternative subjective-ill-will theory remains undecided. Intent, comparability, irrationality, liability and damages remain unproved; no general administrative tort or substantive-due-process right is created.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The pleading judgment is affirmed unanimously and the claim may proceed through ordinary adjudication. Breyer's judgment vote does not add a ninth join to the objective rule. No damages or injunction is awarded.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Sioux City Bridge Co. v. Dakota County: applied for equal protection of an individual against intentional unequal administration, without requiring a separately defined group.
- Allegheny Pittsburgh Coal Co. v. County Commission: applied for deliberate disparate treatment of similarly situated persons; its principle is not limited to a showing of subjective spite.
- FCC v. Beach Communications: its reasonably conceivable legitimate-ground rule, challenger burden and rejection of compulsory formal findings remain.
- Heller v. Doe: applied for the rational relationship to the actual disadvantage; relevant material differences and ordinary government latitude remain distinct from irrational selection.
- Romer v. Evans: applied for objective evaluation of the imposed disadvantage without a required finding about every actor's subjective hostility; no heightened tier is added.



### Municipal policymaking, training and supervision

#### Carter v. City of Philadelphia

**Docket or dockets:** Third Circuit No. 98-1581; no Supreme Court docket supplied.

**Decided:** March 13, 2000.

##### Whether the Philadelphia District Attorney's own-prosecutor administration is local policy and protected by Pennsylvania's immunity

**Holding:** Pennsylvania's sovereign immunity does not bar the claims challenging this Philadelphia office's training, supervision and administrative policy. For training and supervision of the office's own prosecutors, the District Attorney supplies final local policy under Pennsylvania law; neither conclusion classifies every prosecutorial function or establishes authority over police.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, joined by all seven other Associate Justices; Stone-Zsela concurs in the judgment only.

**Material application:** Pennsylvania law, local office control and the City's primary responsibility for judgments establish the relevant local institution. Election, title, territory, funding or final discretion alone would not suffice. The County-officer designation has a home-rule and optional-government exception; the decision does not depend on that label. Defined state intervention for resource insufficiency, conflict or judicially established failure or refusal amounting to abuse does not establish ordinary state control of training.

##### What fault, notice and causal connection a municipal training or supervision omission requires

**Holding:** Carter must prove a federal deprivation attributable to a municipal policy or legally effective custom, a deliberate or conscious training or supervision omission amounting to deliberate indifference, and an identified deficiency closely related to and actually causing his injury. Notice may arise from an established pattern or a sufficiently obvious need to address a clear constitutional duty in known recurring circumstances; prior identical incidents are not invariably required.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, joined by all seven other Associate Justices; Stone-Zsela concurs in the judgment only.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Negligence, employee wrongdoing and hindsight that more training might help do not satisfy municipal fault or cause. Perjury's obvious wrongfulness alone does not show an obvious need for specialized instruction. Any police-control theory requires actual authority and causal proof; cooperation alone creates no employment relationship.

##### Whether heightened pleading can be demanded for this municipal-policy claim

**Holding:** The then-operative Rule 8 pleading standard governs this municipal claim without a judge-created demand for heightened factual particularity about internal policies before discovery. The alleged pattern and policy-related omissions suffice against the categorical dismissal grounds presented, while the substantive liability elements and ordinary procedural controls remain fully applicable.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, joined by all seven other Associate Justices; Stone-Zsela concurs in the judgment only.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Rule 11, managed discovery and Rule 56 remain available. Municipal deliberate-indifference allegations do not automatically defeat personal qualified immunity, which depends on clearly established law at the time of the conduct. A municipality cannot borrow personal immunity; otherwise protected advocacy does not lose its functional protection merely through an allegation of dishonesty.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No misconduct, innocence, actual policy, policymaker knowledge, pattern, supervisory control over police, deliberate indifference, causation or damages is found. The Court does not classify all Pennsylvania officials or all District Attorney functions, decide a new Rule 54(b) rule, resolve the annotated State supersession procedure, or impose particular personnel safeguards. The personal and state-law rulings outside the two granted questions receive no new judgment here.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Affirm reinstatement of the municipal-policy claim within the two granted questions and remand for ordinary proceedings. Liability, damages, any trial and particular safeguards remain unestablished; personal and state-law matters outside the grant receive no new disposition.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- **McMillian v. Monroe County:** Applies its final-authority and governmental-identity inquiry to Pennsylvania's own legal structure. Its Alabama application does not determine every State or every prosecutorial function.
- **Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp.:** Applies the complete structural inquiry; treasury exposure remains highly probative rather than indispensable.
- **Regents of the University of California v. Doe:** Distinguishes a State's primary obligation with collateral indemnity from this independent local office's obligations; the antecedent structural inquiry remains necessary.
- **Monell v. Department of Social Services:** Preserves the requirement of the municipality's own policy or legally effective custom and rejects employer-based liability.
- **City of Canton v. Harris:** Applies deliberate indifference, notice, an identified deficiency and actual causal connection; no universal identical-incident prerequisite or relaxed fault standard is added.
- **Collins v. City of Harker Heights:** Preserves the separate inquiries into a federal deprivation and municipal responsibility.
- **Plakas v. Drinski:** Applies the distinct deprivation, attribution, fault and causal requirements and the separation between personal immunity and municipal liability.
- **Leatherman v. Tarrant County Narcotics Intelligence and Coordination Unit:** Applies ordinary municipal pleading under the Rules and preserves distinct discovery and proof controls.
- **Conley v. Gibson:** Supplies fair-notice pleading under the Rules in force for this action.
- **Buckley v. Fitzsimmons:** Preserves the functional distinction between investigation or administration and protected advocacy; classification of an individual act remains separate.
- **Fletcher v. Kalina:** Preserves otherwise protected advocacy and separate personal evidentiary acts, without a general dishonesty exception or automatic loss of qualified immunity.
- **Chalfin v. Specter, Specter v. Moak, and Duggan v. 807 Liberty Avenue:** Supply their stated Pennsylvania structural classifications; none alone decides federal attribution or every office function.
- **Walker v. City of New York:** Its lower-court elaboration does not become a separate binding Supreme Court test; Canton governs.



### Private enforcement of Title VI disparate-impact regulations

#### Powell v. Ridge

**Docket or dockets:** No Supreme Court docket supplied; review of 189 F.3d 387 (Third Circuit).

**Decided:** April 3, 2000.

##### Whether Title VI implies the impact-regulation action asserted in Count I

**Holding:** Title VI does not create a directly implied private action to enforce this §602 regulation's disparate-impact prohibition merely because the regulation validly implements the statutory program. Section 601's established private protection against intentional discrimination and §602's authority for agency implementation do not show congressional creation of the broader impact-only private remedy asserted here.

**Proposition-level authority:** Thomas's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia and Kennedy; five direct rationale votes.

**Current-force modification:** Alexander v. Sandoval, April 24, 2001, overrules this direct-action prohibition insofar as it excludes prospective enforcement by Title VI beneficiaries of valid, sufficiently definite section 602 requirements implementing their statutory discrimination protection. Plaintiffs must prove the actual regulatory elements and obtain fitted relief. Powell's separate section 1983 holding, completed judgment and distinction between regulatory validity and a congressional source of action remain; Sandoval decides no damages remedy for unintentional effects and reopens no final judgment.

**Later-authority backlinks:** Alexander v. Sandoval, No. 99-1908, April 24, 2001: prospective Title VI enforcement and express partial overruling of the Count I direct-action rule.

##### Whether the regulation creates the individual statutory effects right asserted under section 1983 in Count II

**Holding:** Count II fails independently because §601's intentional-discrimination protection and §602's instructions to agencies do not confer the broader individual statutory right against disparate impact asserted here. A regulation may elaborate an existing statutory entitlement, but this regulation cannot by itself create the missing broader right for §1983 to enforce; rejection rests on right creation, not congressional foreclosure of an established right.

**Proposition-level authority:** Thomas's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia and Kennedy; five direct rationale votes.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The children's alleged comparative treatment injury presents the controversy; the Court does not dismiss for lack of Article III standing. Prospective state officers are not categorically excluded as nonpersons, but the judgment establishes no defendant's liability or entitlement to relief. The municipal plaintiffs' separate standing is unnecessary to the decision.

Section 100.3(b)(2) concerns a covered recipient's criteria or methods of administering services, aid, benefits or facilities that cause the prohibited discrimination or defeat or substantially impair program objectives for protected individuals. It is not a prohibition of every statistical disparity. The Court decides no regulatory validity, recipient coverage, discriminatory purpose, causal funding effect, trial burden framework or statewide allocation requirement. Gebser and Davis govern attribution of intentional discrimination in their own settings and do not create this effects right. Properly presented intentional-discrimination claims remain subject to their own requirements.

Agency termination or refusal of assistance remains subject to an express finding after a hearing opportunity, confined to the recipient and program or part found noncompliant; advice of noncompliance and inability to secure voluntary compliance; and a report to the appropriate congressional committees followed by thirty days before termination or refusal becomes effective. Other means authorized by law remain distinct. General rules remain subject to §602's statutory consistency and presidential-approval requirements. This judgment orders no agency enforcement action.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Reverse both impact-only private theories 5–4 and remand accordingly. There is no separately pleaded section 601 count; genuinely preserved intentional-discrimination theories or ordinary amendment requests retain only their actual procedural footing. No new claim, guaranteed amendment, funding cutoff, finding of nondiscrimination or liability is created.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Cannon v. University of Chicago preserves the established private-action setting for the statutory protection; it does not automatically supply a private action for the broader effects condition.
- Guardians Association v. Civil Service Commission and Alexander v. Choate preserve the statutory/regulatory distinction; their divided positions and remedial assumptions are not converted into an express majority holding on the private channels resolved here.
- Blessing v. Freestone supplies the particular-right inquiry and separate foreclosure analysis. Its allowance for qualitative entitlements and regulatory elaboration remains.
- Suter v. Artist M. preserves provision-specific rights and distinct direct-action analysis; it supplies no categorical immunity for funding statutes.
- Wright v. Roanoke and Wilder v. Virginia Hospital Association retain enforceable individual statutory entitlements and authorized elaboration, distinguished from creation of the additional effects right here.
- Doe v. District of Columbia supplies the distinction between a binding CAPTA agency command and the personal right asserted under §1983.
- Bruneau v. South Kortright Central School District preserves enforcement of an identified Title IX right without enlarging its substantive duty; administrative funding oversight alone is not automatic foreclosure.
- Gebser and Davis retain their intentional-discrimination attribution holdings; their recipient-responsibility rules do not decide this impact-only theory.
- NCAA v. Smith preserves the requirement of actual federal-assistance receipt separately from economic connection, without resolving coverage here.
- Will and Ex parte Young preserve the distinction between prospective relief against state officers and a categorical nonperson objection; they establish no merits liability.



### Individual arms right and official-use firearm disability

#### Gillespie v. City of Indianapolis

**Docket or dockets:** No. 99-626; Seventh Circuit No. 98-2691, reported at 185 F.3d 693.
**Decided:** April 17, 2000.

##### The personal arms right permits this qualifying official-use disability

**Holding:** The Second Amendment protects individuals independently of organized-militia participation, including protected keeping and bearing for work, but section 922(g)(9)'s qualifying domestic-violence disability satisfies intermediate scrutiny on this developed official-use record. The adjudicated violent-conduct predicate, defined domestic relationship, conviction safeguards and statutory limits substantially connect this substantial regulation of particular persons to preventing armed recurrence; the personal right does not require an official-use exemption.

**Proposition-level authority:** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela's unanimous opinion of the Court.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 921(a)(33) requires a federal or state misdemeanor with an element of use or attempted use of physical force, or threatened use of a deadly weapon, committed by a current or former spouse, parent or guardian; a person sharing a child; a current or former cohabitant as spouse, parent or guardian; or a similarly situated person. Counsel or knowing and intelligent waiver is required. Where the jurisdiction grants a jury entitlement, trial or knowing and intelligent waiver by plea or otherwise is required; no new entitlement is created.

A conviction does not count if expunged or set aside, pardoned, or subject to restored civil rights where the jurisdiction provides for their loss for that offense, subject to the express reservation for a pardon, expungement or restoration that expressly prohibits firearm shipment, transportation, possession or receipt. The reservation does not separately repeat set-aside; the Court does not enlarge it. The official text's reference in subsection (a)(33)(A) to subparagraph (C), where the listed safeguards appear in (B), supplies no invented exception; qualification is undisputed here.

Section 925(a)(1)'s governmental channels concern items imported for, sold or shipped to, or issued for use of the United States or its departments or agencies, or a State or its departments, agencies or political subdivisions. It expressly excepts sections 922(d)(9), 922(g)(9) and restrictions concerning section 922(p) firearms. It is not an exemption for every private firearm of a public employee. Section 922(d)'s separate exception for section 925(b) licensees or recipients of section 925(c) relief supplies no general officer exemption. Section 925(b) concerns specified importers, manufacturers, dealers or collectors under indictment for a crime punishable by more than one year, continuing under an existing license with timely renewal where required, during indictment and until conviction becomes final. Section 925(c)'s discretionary public-safety/public-interest relief and review of an actual denial establish no funded process, actual denial, judicial jurisdiction or relief entitlement here.

**Material application:** Intermediate scrutiny requires an important objective, a substantial fit and preservation against unnecessary or effective elimination of protected activity. The accepted qualifying conviction and developed official-use record meet that inquiry. The serious employment burden is not incidental regulation, but individual presentation supplies no material distinction from the same official-use disability previously sustained.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No ordinary home-possession application, defective classification or safeguards, restoration denial, public-carry licensing, training or recertification question is decided. The ungranted equality claim, abandoned fundamental-employment theory and waived felon/misdemeanant comparison remain outside review. The right supplies no unconditional entitlement to this armed public job.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The civil dismissal is affirmed on the controlling individual-right framework. No discharge, reinstatement, reassignment, restoration procedure or new hearing is ordered.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Love is applied to personal invocation; its recognition of the holder supplies no immunity from justified regulation.
- Hale is applied to coverage distinct from regulation and to the necessary-inclusion method; its machinegun holdings do not replace the particular recipient/supply analysis.
- Wright is applied through FOP's specific substantial-regulation holding; its full practical-burden inquiry, home boundary and reserved applications remain unchanged, and it creates no automatic-remand rule.
- Fraternal Order of Police, October 7, 1998, is applied to the qualifying official-use disability; personal rather than associational presentation does not distinguish that controlling application.

For the commerce and municipal-staffing holdings in Gillespie, April 17, 2000, No. 99-626, see Constitutional Structure — Prohibited firearm recipients and municipal staffing.



### State action in private involuntary commitment

#### Doe v. Rosenberg

**Docket or dockets:** Second Circuit No. 98-7803, reported at 166 F.3d 507; district No. 97 CIV. 3205(RWS); no separate Supreme Court docket supplied.
**Decided:** April 24, 2000.

##### Regulation and permission do not alone make this private confinement the State's act

**Holding:** Private physicians' and a private hospital's independently exercised commitment decisions are not attributable to the State merely because a statute authorizes confinement, the institution is extensively regulated, and judicial review is available. Attribution requires a sufficient governmental connection to the particular challenged act, such as coercion, significant encouragement, joint participation or delegation of a traditionally exclusive governmental function; none is established for either identified decision here.

**Proposition-level authority:** All nine Justices join Justice Kennedy's opinion and both applications of this rule.

**Material application:** Neither the referral and hospital-security transport nor the separate private certifications establish public participation. Section 9.27's admission permission and two examining-physician certificates, with subsection (d)'s alternatives requirement, constrain private choice without commanding this confinement. The statutory definitions and judicial dangerousness construction remain distinct.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court decides neither dangerousness nor the validity of confinement. It recognizes no categorical immunity for private hospitals; actual public direction, joint action or delegation of an exclusive governmental duty remains subject to its own proof. Judicial release does not make the earlier private decisions governmental retroactively.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Federal summary judgment is affirmed for both sets of challenged acts. Pendent state claims remain dismissed without a merits decision under section 1367(c)(3); the ungranted discovery ruling stands. The mandate orders no discovery or hearing.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Sullivan is applied to responsibility for the particular private decision; its payment setting is not treated as automatic resolution of confinement.
- Blum and Rendell-Baker are applied for the distinction between regulation and governmental responsibility for a challenged act.
- Lugar retains separate legal-authorization and governmental-attribution requirements; state-created permission alone does not satisfy both.
- West is distinguished because no entrusted governmental custodial duty is established here; professional discretion does not negate attribution when that duty is actually delegated.
- Edmonson is distinguished because this record lacks the governmental machinery and participation present in its jury-function setting.
- Carter retains deprivation, attribution, culpability and causation as separate requirements; its pleading decision supplies no new discovery entitlement in this summary-judgment case.



### Affirmative interference, conduct-time immunity and municipal responsibility

#### Saenz v. Heldenfels Brothers, Inc.

**Docket or dockets:** No separate Supreme Court docket supplied; Fifth Circuit No. 98-40902; review of 183 F.3d 389.
**Decided:** May 9, 2000.

##### I. An official's actual interference with available protection must be distinguished from failure to supply protection

**Holding:** An affirmative command that actually interrupts an available lawful protective response and thereby creates or materially increases exposure to a known danger can present an official-deprivation claim when the required constitutional culpability and attributable causation are established. Such a claim cannot be excluded merely because the injured people were outside custody, their identities were unknown when the command issued, or a private person inflicted the immediate injury; an instruction without that protective and causal effect or the requisite culpability remains insufficient.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part I of Breyer's opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg; five Justices.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The qualifying account concerns knowing, arbitrary suppression of actual protection against an appreciated serious and immediate danger. The Court fixes no minimum culpability standard for lesser accounts, no fifteen-minute threshold, and no duty to investigate or arrest. An unused discretionary protective opportunity or an instruction without actual causal effect remains insufficient.

##### II-A. Individual immunity requires its own conduct-time inquiry

**Holding:** Gonzalez's individual qualified immunity must be determined by whether all relevant law available on June 19, 1995 made the particular conduct's federal unlawfulness apparent to a reasonable officer on the properly supported favorable account. No identical prior collision or Supreme-Court-only precedent is required, but later recognition of a constitutional application cannot supply earlier notice, and recognition of a possible claim does not itself deny immunity.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part II-A of Breyer's opinion, joined by all eight other Justices; nine Justices adopt the method, not a common result applying it.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No controlling rationale resolves immunity for the entire qualifying favorable account: Breyer, Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg would reject categorical immunity, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas would sustain it, and Stone-Zsela reserves application. The opposed outcomes are not a logical-subset relationship under Marks. No mandatory merits-first or immunity-first sequence follows.

##### III. The County's derivative judgment must be reconsidered without merging immunity and municipal responsibility

**Holding:** Because the categorical no-deprivation ground is displaced, Brooks County's judgment resting on that ground must be vacated and reconsidered under the proper constitutional rule. Liability still requires the County's own policy or custom, lawful attribution and causal connection to a federal deprivation; Gonzalez's personal immunity, if established, neither supplies those elements nor independently disposes of the county claim.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part III of Breyer's opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg; five Justices.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court makes no final finding about the command's truth, Gonzalez's actual awareness, the availability and lawfulness of intervention, arbitrary culpability, causal increase of danger, whether an investigation would have prevented the collision, county custom or attribution, private participation, or damages. No general noncustodial danger test, minimum fault rule for every lesser account, duty to arrest, automatic known-victim requirement or police operating protocol is adopted. The individual immunity application lacks a majority holding and remains subject to the stated method.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Vacate the individual and county federal summary judgments, 5–4, for the separate constitutional, June 19, 1995 notice, and municipal-attribution inquiries. Preserve genuine independent grounds, state-law severance and the absence of a new private-company disposition. Vacatur guarantees no discovery, trial, damages or ultimate liability.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services, 489 U.S. 189, retains the rejection of a general protective duty; it does not make the private source of immediate injury dispositive of an official's own affirmative deprivation.
- Pinder v. Johnson, May 21, 1996, preserves the distinction between omission and actual loss of available protection. Applying that distinction to a superior's public-response command is addressed here; Pinder did not already establish liability on these facts. Its different conduct-date immunity judgment remains intact.
- Daniels v. Williams, 474 U.S. 327, continues to exclude negligence; this decision does not resolve every lesser culpability theory reserved in that case.
- County of Sacramento v. Lewis, May 26, 1998, retains its rapid-pursuit harmful-purpose rule and its attention to actual deliberation conditions. It is not extended to every vehicle-related injury or turned into a numerical time rule.
- City of Florence v. Chipman / Stemler v. City of Florence, June 1, 1998, remains a direct-restraint and involuntary-transfer holding with personal knowledge, causal and response limits; those predicates are not supplied here.
- Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800, and Anderson v. Creighton, 483 U.S. 635, retain objective, particularized conduct-time immunity without a factual-twin requirement.
- Elder v. Holloway, February 23, 1994, requires all relevant preconduct authority and preserves ordinary factual and preservation limits. Lanier's later fair-warning explanation supplies no retrospective notice.
- Uhlrig v. Harder, February 18, 1997, retains its different individual-notice disposition and reserved merits; no mandatory sequencing or general danger test is imported.
- Monell v. Department of Social Services, 436 U.S. 658, Collins v. City of Harker Heights, February 26, 1992, and City of Los Angeles v. Heller, 475 U.S. 796, preserve the distinction between federal deprivation, municipal responsibility and a personal immunity defense.
- Freeman, Wood, Ross, Salas, Gregory, Piotrowski and the May 30, 1995 en banc Pinder opinion are considered as contemporaneous circuit authority at their actual holdings and reservations. They are not converted wholesale into Supreme Court rules, and neither side's competing notice application controls merely by collecting their citations.

### Abortion method prohibitions and necessary-health protection

#### Stenberg v. Carhart, 530 U.S. 914 (2000)

**Docket or dockets:** No. 99-830.

**Decided:** June 28, 2000.

##### 1. The complete Casey standard governs the enacted duty and proved applications

**Holding:** The complete six-step Casey standard, as applied in Fargo and Voinovich, governs Nebraska's method prohibition; an established substantial obstacle and denial of timely necessary life-and-health care are independently invalid, and the absence of an obstacle does not end review of remaining severe or meaningful interference. The Court applies that existing rule without substituting a numerical facial threshold, a no-valid-applications barrier, a physician-preference exemption or a new bodily-autonomy framework.

**Proposition-level authority:** Souter's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Ginsburg and Breyer; six direct joins. Kennedy does not join the completed applications.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The complete six-step standard remains in the Casey entry. This decision applies baseline, obstacle and necessary-care protections; it makes no additional obstructive-purpose finding or new residual-interference application. A different precise method restriction with usable care safeguards remains subject to the complete framework.

**Material application:** Before viability the patient decides whether to continue pregnancy without proving medical necessity or obtaining official approval of her reasons. The State may not prohibit that choice, confer effective control on another person, or prevent timely necessary life-and-health care. After viability, prohibition requires the life-and-health safeguard, including individualized physical and mental health considerations. Viability is individualized and medically supported, not a fixed constitutional week. Clinical appropriateness concerns safe and suitable care, not official approval of the patient's reasons; not every preference is a medical emergency.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Challengers establish the duty, population, causation and triggering interference. The State then bears the applicable justification and tailoring or fit burden. This does not alter ordinary proof of disputed historical facts or the enacted burden for a separate statutory defense. No State substantiation burden arises merely because a law concerns abortion.

##### 2. The enacted definition reaches ordinary D&E and creates a substantial obstacle

**Holding:** Nebraska's definition reaches the supported ordinary dilation-and-evacuation sequence when the physician deliberately and intentionally brings a living fetus or a substantial portion into the vagina to perform a procedure the physician knows will cause death and that does cause death before delivery is completed. Prohibiting those ordinary D&E applications removes practical access to the predominant second-trimester method for the affected previability patients and creates a substantial obstacle, independently sustaining the existing bounded declaration and injunction.

**Proposition-level authority:** Souter's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Ginsburg and Breyer; six direct joins. Kennedy does not join the completed applications.

**Material application:** The enacted substantial-portion alternative reaches the described living-limb D&E sequence when all intent, knowledge, life and timing elements are met. The Court does not prohibit every D&E by label or treat removal after death as satisfying the living-fetus requirement.
